name: Mystic Massacre
nations: Pequot (Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation; Eastern Pequot Tribal Nation)
perpetrators: Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay forces under John Mason and John Underhill
linked_instrument: Treaty of Hartford, 1638 (colonial; no federal cession record)
link_note: Colonial era: no Royce area records this land.
citation: worldhistory.org Mystic Massacre of 1637
summary: Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay forces under John Mason and John Underhill, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, burned the fortified Pequot village at Mystic and killed those who fled. The 1638 Hartford treaty divided Pequot survivors and land among the victors and barred use of the Pequot name.
evidence_display: Reported by worldhistory.org Mystic Massacre of 1637

name: Conestoga killings
other_names: Conestoga Town and the Lancaster workhouse; Paxton Boys
deaths_source: Benjamin Franklin, Narrative of the Late Massacres (1764)
linked_instrument: Conestoga Manor (proprietary grant); no cession instrument
link_note: Colonial era: no Royce area records this land.
citation: Benjamin Franklin, A Narrative of the Late Massacres in Lancaster County (1764)
quote: hearing that the remaining fourteen Indians were in the Work-houfc at Lancajler
summary: Paxton Boys (about 50 mounted settlers) killed 6 Conestoga at Conestoga Town, then on Dec 27 broke into the Lancaster workhouse and killed the 14 survivors held there for protection: 20 dead, the last of the community. No one was prosecuted.

name: Gnadenhutten Massacre
linked_instrument: Treaty of Greenville, 1795 (7 Stat. 49)
link_note: A time sequence only: no source ties the killings to the cession.
citation: Wikipedia 'Gnadenhutten massacre
summary: Pennsylvania militia under David Williamson seized about 96 unarmed Moravian Lenape and Mohican, voted to kill them, and killed them over a day. The Tuscarawas villages were never reoccupied by the Lenape; the area fell within later Ohio cessions.

name: Tallushatchee
linked_instrument: Treaty of Fort Jackson, 1814 (7 Stat. 120)
link_note: The Fort Jackson treaty demands the cession as an equivalent for the expenses of the war.
citation: Encyclopedia of Alabama, Battle of Tallushatchee; 7 Stat. 120; Kappler II 107
quote: In all, 186 Red Sticks were killed, including a number of women and children.
summary: Gen. John Coffee's Tennessee militia (under Andrew Jackson) surrounded Tallushatchee and killed the town's men and some women and children; it opened the campaign that ended at Horseshoe Bend and the Fort Jackson cession.

name: Tohopeka (Horseshoe Bend)
perpetrators: Andrew Jackson's army with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies
linked_instrument: Treaty of Fort Jackson, 1814 (7 Stat. 120)
link_note: The Fort Jackson treaty demands the cession as an equivalent for the expenses of the war.
citation: NPS Horseshoe Bend NMP, History & Culture; 7 Stat. 120; Kappler II 107
quote: By dark at least 800 of Chief Menawa's 1,000 Red Sticks were dead (557 slain on the field and 200-300 in the river).
summary: Jackson's army with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies destroyed the fortified Red Stick town of Tohopeka. Five months later Jackson dictated the Fort Jackson cession of about 20 to 23 million acres, signed largely by Creek leaders who had been US allies.

name: Bad Axe Massacre
perpetrators: U.S. regulars, militia and the steamboat Warrior
linked_instrument: Treaty of Fort Armstrong, 1832 (7 Stat. 374)
link_note: The treaty takes the land "partly as indemnity" for the war and holds Black Hawk and others as hostages.
citation: Treaty with the Sauk and Foxes, 1832, preamble (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 374; Kappler II 349
quote: partly as indemnity for the expense incurred, and partly to secure the
summary: At Bad Axe (Aug. 1-2, 1832) US troops, militia and the steamboat Warrior attacked Black Hawk's band, mostly families, at the Mississippi crossing; at least 150 died, with estimates up to about 300, and others drowned or were killed by Dakota across the river. Seven weeks later the 1832 treaty took the Iowa strip (Royce 175) expressly "partly as indemnity" for the war and held Black Hawk and others as hostages. The 400-square-mile reserve (Royce 226) was kept in 1832 and ceded in 1836.

name: Sacramento River Massacre
perpetrators: John C. Fremont's expedition, with settlers
linked_instrument: No ratified treaty
link_note: No treaty ever ceded this land; California's 1851-52 treaties were never ratified.
citation: Wikipedia 'Sacramento River massacre
summary: John C. Fremont's US Army topographical expedition, with Kit Carson and local settlers, attacked a large gathering of Wintu on the Sacramento River, pinning women and children against the river. It came weeks before the US conquest of Mexican California.

name: Dokdokwas
linked_instrument: Klamath treaty, 1864 (later context, not a consequence)
citation: Oregon History Project (Oregon Historical Society), Fremont and Kit Carson at Upper Klamath Lake; 16 Stat. 707 (context only)
quote: Frémont and Kit Carson attacked and burned a Klamath village, killing 14 men.
summary: In May 1846, after an attack on Fremont's camp, Fremont and Carson attacked and burned a Klamath village at the Williamson River mouth, killing 14 men by Fremont's count (Oregon Historical Society); others say more, including women and children. Date is May 10 in Fremont's memoir account, May 12 in others. The 1864 Klamath treaty is later context, not a consequence.

name: Fort Utah killings
linked_instrument: Act of May 5, 1864 (13 Stat. 63) vacating the Utah reserves
link_note: A time sequence only (14 years). Utah Valley was settled without a ratified cession.
citation: Act of May 5, 1864 (Statutes at Large); Royce 449-452; 13 Stat. 63
quote: An Act to vacate and sell the present Indian Reservations in Utah
summary: In February 1850 the Nauvoo Legion besieged a Timpanogos camp on the Provo River and then killed men who had surrendered or fled (Rock Canyon, Spanish Fork); estimates run from about 40 to over 100 dead. Utah Valley was later settled without a ratified cession; the small reserves of 1856-59 were vacated by the act of May 5, 1864 (13 Stat. 63) and restored to the public domain in 1878.

name: Bloody Island Massacre
perpetrators: U.S. Army under Capt. Nathaniel Lyon and Lt. J. W. Davidson
linked_instrument: Unratified treaty with the Clear Lake bands, Aug. 20, 1851
link_note: The 1851 treaty for this land was never ratified.
citation: Wikipedia 'Bloody Island massacre
summary: US Army dragoons and infantry under Capt. Nathaniel Lyon and Lt. J.W. Davidson killed Pomo who had taken refuge on an island, in reprisal for the killing of Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone, who had enslaved and starved Pomo laborers. The 1851 treaty for the area was never ratified.

name: Yontocket Massacre
deaths_range: about 20 to 600 (450 to 600 in tribal accounts)
deaths_source: Native American Heritage Commission; Tolowa Dee-ni' accounts
linked_instrument: No ratified treaty
link_note: A ceremonial site; the location shown is general. Display to be confirmed with the Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation.
citation: Federal Register NAGPRA notice, Mar. 11, 2014 (79 FR, doc. 2014-05322)
quote: One of the first and most brutal attacks occurred at Yan’daa-k’vt, while the people gathered for the Earth Renewal Ceremony, Nee-dash.
summary: A federal notice (2014), drawing on Tolowa Dee-ni' information, records a massacre at Yan'daa-k'vt (Burnt Ranch) during the Nee-dash ceremony, one of the first attacks of a Tolowa holocaust that began in 1851. Death estimates range widely (NAHC 20-600; often 450-600 in tribal accounts). The row's detail of a summer-solstice dating is one historian's view.

name: Little Butte Creek Massacre
linked_instrument: Treaty with the Rogue River (Table Rock), 1853 (10 Stat. 1018)
link_note: It followed the Table Rock cession and set off the 1855-56 war and the 1856 removal north.
citation: Oregon Encyclopedia (Hungry Hill; Rogue River War) via search; SOHS; 10 Stat. 1018; Kappler II 603
summary: On Oct. 8, 1855, volunteers under James Lupton attacked a Takelma camp near Butte Creek before dawn; estimates run from 23-24 to 40 killed, about half women and children. It set off the 1855-56 Rogue River War and the 1856 removal north. Royce 407 is wrong for this link: 407 is the Grand Ronde reserve set up by executive order of June 30, 1857, not a cession; the Table Rock cession under 10 Stat. 1018 is Royce 312.

name: Jarboe's war on the Yuki
deaths_range: 283 (Jarboe's own report; women and children not counted)
perpetrators: Eel River Rangers under Walter Jarboe, paid by the State of California
linked_instrument: No ratified treaty
citation: Wikipedia 'Mendocino War' and 'Walter S. Jarboe
summary: With Gov. John Weller's permission, Walter Jarboe's Eel River Rangers raided Yuki communities for six months; Jarboe himself reported 283 'warriors' killed, not counting women and children, and the state paid the company. The Yuki were reduced to a few hundred and confined to Round Valley.
evidence_display: Reported by Wikipedia 'Mendocino War' and 'Walter S. Jarboe

name: Tuluwat Massacre
linked_instrument: No ratified treaty
link_note: The City of Eureka returned the island to the Wiyot Tribe in 2019.
citation: Wikipedia; Indianz; Cultural Survival
summary: Settlers attacked Tuluwat on Indian Island during the World Renewal Ceremony and other Wiyot villages the same night (Feb. 26, 1860), killing mostly women, children and elders. Estimates for the night range from about 60 to 250. No Wiyot land was ceded by a ratified treaty; Eureka returned the island to the Wiyot Tribe in 2019.

name: Fort Snelling concentration camp
linked_instrument: Acts of Feb. 16, 1863 (12 Stat. 652) and Mar. 3, 1863 (12 Stat. 819)
link_note: Congress voided the Dakota treaties and took the reserve while Dakota people were held at the camp.
citation: Act of Feb. 16, 1863 (Statutes at Large); MNHS Historic Fort Snelling; 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819
quote: are hereby declared to be abrogated and annulled, so far as said treaties or any of them purport to impose any future obligation on the United States
summary: After the 1862 war (begun amid withheld annuities), about 1,600 Dakota noncombatants were held in a stockade below Fort Snelling where 130 to 300 died; Congress then voided the Dakota treaties, forfeited annuities and land, and ordered removal from Minnesota. The Minnesota River reserve (Royce 440) was taken and sold.

name: Mankato mass execution
linked_instrument: Act of Feb. 16, 1863 (12 Stat. 652)
link_note: A mass execution after military trials; the abrogation followed within weeks (a sequence within the same war response).
citation: MNHS, U.S.-Dakota War: The Trials & Hanging; 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819
quote: On December 26, 1862, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato.
summary: Thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged together after military commission trials, some lasting minutes; it is the largest mass execution in US history and was followed within weeks by treaty abrogation and removal.

name: Whitestone Hill Massacre
nations: Yanktonai Dakota, Hunkpapa Lakota and Dakota refugees
linked_instrument: No cession linked
citation: State Historical Society of North Dakota, Whitestone Hill State Historic Site
quote: Many Indian men, women, and children died or were captured.
summary: Gen. Alfred Sully's troops attacked a large camp gathered to hunt and dry meat, most of whose people had no role in the 1862 Minnesota war, killing 150 to 300 or more and destroying winter food stores.

name: Bear River Massacre
nations: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
deaths_source: Utah Division of Indian Affairs and markers (verification round 2)
perpetrators: California Volunteers under Col. Patrick Edward Connor
linked_instrument: Treaty of Box Elder, July 30, 1863 (13 Stat. 663)
link_note: The Box Elder treaty has no Royce area. Areas 444 and 447 belong to the Western Shoshone and Goshute, not the Northwestern Band.
citation: Royce 1899 entry 444 (Ruby Valley treaty, Western Shoshone); 13 Stat. 663; 18 Stat. 685; 18 Stat. 689
quote: No formal purchase of the territorial claim of these tribes or bands was made, but the U. S. took possession of the same
summary: Connor's California Volunteers attacked the Northwestern Shoshone winter camp at Boa Ogoi on Jan. 29, 1863, killing about 250 to 500 (estimates: about 250, about 350 per Utah Division of Indian Affairs, 400+ on markers). The 1863 Shoshone and Goshute treaties followed within nine months. The Royce quote and areas 444 and 447 concern the Western Shoshone (Ruby Valley) and Goshute, not the Northwestern Band, whose Box Elder treaty (13 Stat. 663) has no Royce area. The massacre-to-treaty link is a time sequence; no source here says the massacre caused those treaties.

name: Owens Valley killings
link_note: Round 2: the specific killings are not yet sourced; do not map a point.
citation: Wikipedia 'Moses A. McLaughlin
summary: During the Owens Valley war of 1862-63 settlers and California Volunteers killed Paiute in several attacks, including a massacre of about 35 attributed to Capt. Moses McLaughlin. Over 1,000 Paiute were then marched about 200 miles to Fort Tejon in July 1863; by Jan 1864 only 380 remained there, many having fled home.

name: Blue Water Creek Massacre
other_names: Ash Hollow; Battle of Blue Water
deaths_source: Harney's report as usually cited (not checked)
perpetrators: Troops under Gen. William Harney (about 70 women and children taken)
linked_instrument: Harney's council at Fort Pierre, 1856 (never ratified)
quote: He killed eighty-six men women, and children and took seventy hostages
summary: Gen. William Harney attacked Little Thunder's Brule camp, killing about 86 men, women and children and taking about 70 hostages (mostly women and children). Harney then dictated terms to Lakota bands at Fort Pierre in 1856 while captives were held.

name: Poncha Pass attack
location_basis: No location in the sources yet.
nations: Ute (Mouache and Capote) and Jicarilla Apache
linked_instrument: Meriwether treaties, Aug. 1855 (never ratified)
citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 404
quote: capturing over 50 women and children, who were probably placed in Anglo and Mexican households as slaves.
summary: Col. Thomas Fauntleroy surprised a camp near Poncha Pass on April 28, 1855, killing forty warriors. The campaign then destroyed lodges and captured over 50 women and children, probably placed as slaves in Anglo and Mexican households. Some sources report mutilation and Ute women killing their children to avoid capture.

name: Cedar Canyon attack
location_basis: No location in the sources yet (about sixty miles north of the South Platte).
citation: Testimony of Jacob Downing, Condition of the Indian Tribes; S. Rep. No. 156 (1867), App. 69
quote: I captured an Indian and required him to go to the village, or I would kill him.
summary: Maj. Jacob Downing testified that in mid-May 1864 he forced a captured Indian to guide him "or I would kill him", surprised a Cheyenne village at Cedar Bluffs about sixty miles north of the South Platte, killed (as he was told) about 26 and wounded 30, burned the lodges, took no prisoners, and gave the captured stock to his men. The pyre threat and the identification of the captive as Spotted Horse are not in Downing's testimony. The campaign followed a dispute over the rancher Ripley's stock, not a single stolen horse.

name: Sand Creek Massacre
perpetrators: 1st and 3rd Colorado Cavalry under Col. John Chivington
linked_instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct. 14, 1865 (14 Stat. 703)
link_note: The survivors gave up the Fort Wise reserve eleven months later in a treaty that itself acknowledged the outrages.
citation: Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War, Massacre of Cheyenne Indians (1865); JCCW, 38th Cong. 2d sess. (1865), Massacre of Cheyenne Indians pp. I-VI
quote: he surprised and murdered, in cold blood, the unsuspecting men, women, and children on Sand creek, who had every reason to believe they were under the protection of the United States
summary: The Joint Committee found that Chivington "surprised and murdered, in cold blood" people who had every reason to believe they were under U.S. protection, and found Evans's testimony marked by "prevarication and shuffling". It called for removing from office "those who have thus disgraced the government", without naming Evans. That Evans bore more responsibility than anyone is TREC's view.

name: Washita Massacre
perpetrators: 7th Cavalry under Lt. Col. George Custer
linked_instrument: Medicine Lodge treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867 (15 Stat. 593)
link_note: NPS: the loss of winter supplies forced many bands to accept reservation life. The 1867 cession has no Royce area in the atlas.
citation: NPS, Washita Battlefield NHS, History & Culture; 15 Stat. 593; Kappler II 984
quote: quickly retreated to Camp Supply with his captives - 53 women and children
summary: Custer's troops took 53 Cheyenne women and children captive at the Washita (NPS). NPS says the loss of winter supplies "forced many bands to accept reservation life". The claim that the captives were used as hostages or human shields to drive bands onto the reservation is historians' interpretation not found in the NPS page; attribute it to the named historian before mapping as HOSTAGE.

name: Summit Springs
location_basis: No location in the sources yet.
linked_instrument: Medicine Lodge treaty, 1867
link_note: Berthrong (as quoted in PSL TREC): it ended Cheyenne occupation of the Platte-Arkansas country.
citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 218
quote: The Battle of Summit Springs thus ended Cheyenne occupation and use of the region between the Platte and Arkansas rivers.
summary: Maj. Carr's troops defeated the Dog Soldiers at Summit Springs, killing 52 including Tall Bull. Berthrong: this ended Cheyenne occupation of the region between the Platte and Arkansas.

name: Marias Massacre
linked_instrument: Executive order of July 5, 1873 and Act of Apr. 15, 1874
link_note: A time sequence only: no source ties the reductions to the massacre.
citation: Montana Historical Society (IEFA lesson; Henderson, Montana Magazine 2018) via search; 18 Stat. 28 [unchecked]; 25 Stat. 113
summary: Baker's 2nd Cavalry attacked Heavy Runner's Piikani camp on Jan. 23, 1870, not the band sought; the Army's count was 173 dead, mostly women, children and elders, and Henderson gives 217. Coordinates in the row (48.4,-111.1) are about 40 km east of the usually given site (about 48.39,-111.66, near the Marias in Toole/Pondera area). The 1873-74 reductions followed but no source here ties them to the massacre.

name: Camp Grant Massacre
perpetrators: Tucson party of Anglo-Americans, Mexican Americans and Tohono O'odham
linked_instrument: Camp Grant reserve, executive order of Nov. 9, 1871; revoked Dec. 14, 1872
link_note: A time sequence only.
citation: HistoryNet; True West; Royce 1899 entry 541
quote: President restores to public domain reservation established at Camp Grant, Nov. 9, 1871.
summary: On Apr. 30, 1871 a Tucson party of Anglo-Americans, Mexican Americans and Tohono O'odham attacked Aravaipa and Pinal Apache families under Army protection, killing about 85 to 144, mostly women and children, and taking 27 to 30 children. A Camp Grant reserve was approved Nov. 9, 1871 and restored to the public domain Dec. 14, 1872 (Royce 541). The reserve was not a cession, and the massacre-to-reserve link is a sequence.

name: Attack on Morning Star's village
other_names: Red Fork of the Powder River; Dull Knife Fight
location_basis: No location in the sources yet.
deaths_range: not established (a village of 173 lodges burned)
linked_instrument: Agreement of 1876, Act of Feb. 28, 1877 (19 Stat. 254)
quote: U.S. troops found them and burned their village.
summary: US troops found and burned the 173-lodge Northern Cheyenne village, destroying winter supplies; the source says it affected the Cheyenne more than Little Bighorn. Starvation forced surrenders in spring 1877.

name: Big Hole
perpetrators: 7th Infantry under Col. John Gibbon and volunteers
linked_instrument: Nez Perce treaty, June 9, 1863 (14 Stat. 647)
link_note: The bands were in flight after the 1877 order to move onto the reduced 1863 reservation.
citation: NPS Big Hole National Battlefield; 14 Stat. 647; Kappler II 843
quote: Between 60 and 90 nımí·pu· men, women, and children were killed during the battle
summary: Gibbon's troops and volunteers attacked the sleeping Nimiipuu camp at dawn on Aug. 9, 1877, killing 60 to 90 men, women and children; 31 soldiers and volunteers died (NPS). The "only about 30 were warriors" figure was not found in the NPS pages read. The bands were in flight after the 1877 order to move onto the reduced 1863 reservation.

name: Fort Robinson breakout and killings
location_basis: No location in the sources yet.
deaths_range: 64 (Army count) and higher in Cheyenne accounts
deaths_source: Commissioner of Indian Affairs report; Army count (verification round 2)
linked_instrument: Forced second removal of the Northern Cheyenne
link_note: Prisoners were held without food or fuel to force their return south.
citation: ARCIA 1879, Commissioner's report; Grinnell 1915; ARCIA 1879, p. XVII
quote: They were pursued by the troops, and most of their number were eventually killed.
summary: On the night of Jan. 9, 1879 the starving prisoners broke out; troops pursued and, by the Commissioner's own account, "most of their number were eventually killed". The same report says the prisoners had at least 15 guns and killed two sentinels. Grinnell records about fifty bodies brought in. The Army's 64 dead / 78 captured / 7 missing count, the Jan. 22 washout volleys and the civilian killings come from the Board of Officers proceedings, which were not reached.

name: Posse and Guard attack near Meeker
location_basis: No location in the sources yet.
perpetrators: Garfield County posse, volunteers and the Colorado National Guard
linked_instrument: Act of June 15, 1880 (21 Stat. 199)
quote: Eight Ute People had been killed, including a small child and an infant.
summary: Garfield County Sheriff Kendall's posse burned Chipeta's camp; later posse, volunteers and Colorado National Guard attacked the Utes as they returned toward Utah. Eight Utes were killed including a small child and an infant; volunteers stole about 600 horses and 2,500 sheep. Misnamed 'Colorow's War'.

name: Wounded Knee Massacre
nations: Mniconjou and Hunkpapa Lakota (Spotted Elk's band)
deaths_range: at least 250 (186 listed by Joseph Horn Cloud; estimates near 300)
deaths_source: Wounded Knee National Historic Landmark nomination
linked_instrument: Act of Mar. 2, 1889 (25 Stat. 888)
link_note: It came 21 months after the 1889 act and amid ration cuts: context, not a sourced cause.
citation: NPS, Wounded Knee National Historic Landmark nomination; 25 Stat. 888; 19 Stat. 254
quote: A total of at least 250 dead is almost certain.
summary: The 7th Cavalry killed at least 250 Lakota, mostly women, children and elders, while disarming Spotted Elk's band on Dec. 29, 1890; 146 were buried in the mass grave and Joseph Horn Cloud listed 186 dead (NHL nomination), with higher estimates near 300. The 350-375 figure was not verified. It came 21 months after the 1889 act and amid ration cuts; that is context, not a sourced cause of a land taking.
